To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we propose a novel algorithm, VISR, that learns to infer the rewards of new tasks from a single demonstration, using only the intrinsic rewards of the agent.
we introduce VISR, a novel algorithm which combines the benefits of controllable policies and successor features, and that VISR outperforms all baselines in our novel task inference experiments.

(1) VISR, a novel algorithm which combines successor features with intrinsic motivation, achieves state-of-the-art performance in the task of learning from limited rewards, and (2) VISR achieves this performance by learning a controllable feature space, which can be leveraged for task inference and improved generalization.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how to enable agents to rapidly learn from limited reward feedback.
the problem of how to learn a policy in a reinforcement learning setting where the reward function is unknown, but a finite set of tasks is available.
how an agent can learn from its own experience and that of others to perform a variety of tasks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed algorithm is able to solve the task of fast task inference, by learning controllable features that are then used to generalize and provide enhanced performance.
the proposed algorithm is capable of learning from a limited amount of reward information and can be used to quickly adapt to a new task, while maintaining a diverse set of behaviors.
this paper introduces an algorithm that learns to learn from a small number of demonstrations, which is a step toward the ultimate goal of general intelligence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we propose a method to learn a representation for the state-action space, which allows the agent to generalize across a variety of tasks.

we introduce an algorithm which can learn controllable features that generalize well across tasks, and which can be used to rapidly infer the task and learn a policy for the task, even when the rewards are only available after a long unsuervised training phase.

1) VISR is a novel algorithm that can learn to infer tasks in a generalizable manner; 2) We show that VISR can be trained in an unsupervised fashion and still learn to infer tasks; 3) VISR outperforms all baselines in terms of task inference accuracy, and achieves human-level performance on several Atari games.
The main takeaway from our work is that
VISR is able to leverage the controllable behaviors learned in an unsupervised fashion to rapidly learn new tasks.
by combining two seemingly different techniques, we can obtain an agent that can rapidly learn from limited reward feedback.
by combining two seemingly different techniques, VISR is able to learn features that can be reused to quickly adapt to a new task.
